notes.about: Twice the verse says the oppressed had no comforter: after their tears, and after the power of their oppressors. Said again, the words stress their lasting misery and how little pity others showed them. The second can also show why: those who might have comforted them feared the oppressors.

original.note: In Hebrew the two lines are the same words, ve-ein lahem menachem, and there was to them no comforter.

notes.evidence: A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) says no comforter is said twice to express suffering that goes on with none to comfort. Matthew Poole says it is repeated to show both men's great inhumanity to others in trouble and the utter misery of the oppressed. Matthew Henry reads both: they wept with no comforter, and as the oppressors were powerful, those who should comfort them dared not.

cites.quote: no comforter--twice said to express continued suffering without any to give comfort ( Isa 53:7 ).

cites.quote: They had no comforter; which is repeated as an argument both of the great inhumanity of men towards others in calamity, and of the extreme misery of oppressed persons.

They wept and needed comfort, but there was none to do that friendly office: They had no comforter; their oppressors were powerful and threatening, and therefore they had no comforter; those that should have comforted them durst not, for fear of displeasing the oppressors and being made their companions for offering to be their comforters.

notes.short: Sorrow is better, for it does the heart good
notes.about: The first line makes a claim, that sorrow is better than laughter, and the second gives the reason: a sad countenance is good for the heart. Grief that shows in the face can lead a person to search his own conscience and resolve to amend his life.

lines.words: for a sad countenance is good for the heart.

notes.evidence: Adam Clarke says the reason is given at once in the second line: by the sorrow that shows in the face the heart is made better, as men search their own consciences and resolve to amend. Matthew Henry reads the second line as showing that sorrow is also more for our advantage, since by the sadness that appears in the face the heart is often made better.

cites.quote: Sorrow is better than laughter - The reason is immediately given; for by the sorrow of the countenance - the grief of heart that shows itself in the countenance: - The heart is made better - In such cases, most men try themselves at the tribunal of their own consciences, and resolve on amendment of life.
cites.read: sacred-texts.com's transcription, in the copy at github.com/jonnyg23/mahabrain (commit b00aa50)

cites.quote: Sorrow is better than laughter, more agreeable to our present state, where we are daily sinning and suffering ourselves, more or less, and daily seeing the sins and sufferings of others. ... It is also more for our advantage; for, by the sadness that appears in the countenance, the heart is often made better.

notes.short: Extortion and a bribe: two ways wisdom is lost
notes.about: Both lines tell how a wise man is undone. The first says extortion turns him into a fool. The second says a bribe corrupts the heart, that is, his understanding, and so says the same again. Two causes are named, with one result: the wise man loses his wisdom.

lines.words: Surely extortion turns a wise man into a fool,
and a bribe corrupts the heart.

pairs: turns a wise man into a fool

original.note: In Hebrew the heart (lev) often stands for the understanding, so the second line speaks of the wise man's mind.

notes.evidence: Matthew Poole says the bribe deprives the wise man of his understanding, which is often called the heart, or makes him mad, as the first clause said, so the verse shows two ways a wise man may be made mad. A. R. Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) takes the heart as the wisdom the wise may lose, and says this reading suits the parallel lines.
notes.limit: The writers differ on how the wise man meets these things: one by suffering oppression and taking bribes, the other by seeing oppression and bribery done by others.

cites.quote: deprives him of the use of his understanding, which is oft called the heart, ... or makes him mad, as was said in the former clause. So this verse discovers two ways whereby a wise man may be made mad, by suffering oppression from others, or by receiving bribes to oppress others.

a gift--that is, the sight of bribery in "places of judgment" ( Ecc 3:16 ) might cause the wise to lose their wisdom (equivalent to "heart"), ( Job 12:6 ; Job 21:6-7 ; Job 24:1 , &c.). This suits the parallelism better than "a heart of gifts"

notes.short: A saying: “a live dog is better than a dead lion”
notes.about: The verse sets a live dog beside a dead lion in a short saying read as a proverb. While a man lives there is still hope, and even the lowliest life is better than the greatest who has died.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: a live dog is better than a dead lion
figure.means: the lowliest person still alive is better off than the greatest who has died, for the living still have hope

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the words under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. Clarke supposes it was a proverb and explains it: the smallest measure of life is better than the largest of dead matter, and the poorest living peasant is infinitely above Alexander the Great.
notes.limit: The writers differ on where the saying began: one supposes it was already a proverb, the other lists it among sayings first found in Scripture that later passed into common use.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 762
cites.quote: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture; but, which, owing to their fulness of meaning and their wide application, have since passed into general use as proverbial sayings ... “For a living dog is better than a dead lion.”

notes.short: A saying: dead flies spoil the perfumer's oil
notes.about: The verse opens with a picture: dead flies make the perfumer’s oil stink. It then applies it: a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor. The picture is read as a saying first found here that has since passed into common use.

figure.name: Proverb
figure.part: Appear for the first time in Scripture
figure.words: dead flies bring a stench to the perfumer’s oil
figure.means: a small thing can spoil something precious, as the verse says a little folly outweighs wisdom and honor

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists the opening words under Parœmia, among sayings first found in Scripture that have since passed into general use as proverbs. The verse itself gives the application to a little folly.
notes.limit: Only one writer cited here calls the picture a proverb.

cites.at: Parœmiœ which appear for the first time in Scripture, p. 762

notes.short: Old age and death in one long picture
notes.about: The days of adversity in verse 1 are pictured: the lights grow dark, “the keepers of the house tremble”, the watchers at the windows see dimly, the almond tree blossoms. The writers read it as old age, the house as the failing body, and two of them read verse 6 as death.

figure.name: Allegory
figure.words: the keepers of the house tremble
figure.means: the body failing in old age, pictured as a house whose keepers, strong men, grinders and watchers are the hands and arms, legs, teeth and eyes

notes.evidence: Poole calls verse 2 and the verses after it wholly allegorical. W. T. Bullock (Barnes' Notes) says the body in old age and death is pictured as a decaying house; Clarke, that the body is compared to a house; Henry, that old age is described in figurative expressions, and death in verse 6; Fausset (Jamieson, Fausset and Brown) calls verse 6 a double image of death, as verses 1 to 5 are of old age.
notes.limit: The writers differ on verse 6: one reads the silver cord and golden bowl as a hanging lamp whose cord and bowl answer to the spinal marrow and skull; another reads the cord as the bond between soul and body.

cites.quote: which seems not to agree with the context, partly because the dimness of their sight is expressed in the next verse, and partly because both his and the following verses are wholly allegorical.

The body in old age and death is here described under the figure of a decaying house with its inmates and furniture. This verse is best understood as referring to the change which old age brings to four parts of the body, the arms ("the keepers"), the legs ("the strong men"), the teeth ("the grinders"), and the eyes.

cites.quote: The Body of man is here compared to a House: - mark the metaphors and their propriety. 1. The keepers shall tremble - the hands become paralytic, as is constantly the case, less or more, in old age. 2. The strong men shall bow - The legs become feeble, and unable to support the weight of the body.
